The juvenile growth phase of Ram (Planorbis planorbis) begins immediately after the larva undergoes the dramatic process of metamorphosis, a period marked by an allometric shift in body proportions. Following the loss of the velum and settlement to the benthos, the recently metamorphosed juvenile emerges at a shell length of 0.3 centimeters . This morphological transformation occurs after a relatively brief post-hatching interval; at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the transition from the veliger to the juvenile form is completed approximately 22.5 days since birth . The associated wet body mass at this critical developmental stage is remarkably slight, weighing just 0.0088 grams . This low mass reflects the small size of the recently settled individual and the fact that the animal has only recently initiated its exotrophic transition, beginning to feed actively on detritus and periphyton.

As the juvenile snail continues to grow and allocate resources toward somatic development, it eventually reaches a key life-history transition: the attainment of reproductive maturity. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], individuals of Planorbis planorbis reach puberty approximately 47.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 47.5 days since birth]. This timing is dependent on the accumulation of sufficient tissue mass, with the onset of gametogenesis typically recorded once the snail achieves a shell length of 0.72 centimeters [Lp = 0.72 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 0.1216 grams [Wwp = 0.1216 grams], a value that represents the minimal body size required to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and subsequent spawning events in this freshwater pulmonate.

The initial stages of the life cycle in this species are characterized by rapid embryogenesis within the egg mass. Incubation at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] yields a remarkably short developmental period, with hatching occurring after only 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days]. At the moment of emergence, the newly hatched juveniles are quite diminutive, possessing a total shell length of just 0.06 centimeters [Lb = 0.06 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at birth is minuscule, recorded at only 0.00006117 grams [Wwb = 0.00006117 grams], a value that underscores the extreme altricial-like state of the recently hatched Ram. This tiny birth mass is typical for aquatic gastropods that produce large numbers of small, encapsulated embryos, though it is notably lower than that reported for some related planorbid species.

Gravid adults of Planorbis planorbis exhibit a notable reproductive capacity, with the maximum reproductive rate displayed under optimal thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a single reproductively active adult is capable of producing an average of one egg mass per day [Ri = one egg mass per day], with each mass typically containing approximately 10 eggs [N_R_i = each mass typically containing approximately 10 eggs]. This daily egg output, while seemingly modest per event, accumulates rapidly over the extended breeding season and contributes to the species' substantial population turnover. The maximum longevity of individuals maintained in captivity at this same temperature is quite extensive for a small-bodied gastropod; the lifespan, measured as the time from hatching until natural death, reaches 210 days [am = 210 days] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].

The ultimate adult body size of Ram represents the culmination of months of continuous somatic growth following the completion of metamorphosis. Under favorable conditions, sexually mature individuals eventually attain a maximum shell length of approximately 1.1 centimeters [Li = approximately 1.1 centimeters]. The corresponding ultimate wet weight recorded in reproductively active adults is 0.4336 grams [Wwi = 0.4336 grams]. This asymptotic body mass represents the maximum sustainable size for the species in its typical lentic habitats, balancing the biomechanical constraints of shell production against the energetic costs of foraging and reproduction. The transition from the juvenile stage to this adult form involves a roughly seventy-fold increase in wet weight from the 0.00006117 grams [Wwb = 0.00006117 grams] recorded at hatching, a growth trajectory that is fueled by efficient assimilation of epiphytic algae.
